explanations.answer: So no one can discredit their ministry
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says it right in the verse: “We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no one can discredit our ministry.” He wants nothing in how they serve to hand anyone a reason to brush the work aside. I'd sweep my own front step for that.

explanations.answer: So the leaders in Jerusalem approve
explanations.explanation: Close call, baker, but Jerusalem never comes up in these verses. Paul gives his reason right in verse 3: “…so that no one can discredit our ministry.” The text names no leaders and no approval, so I won't hand them a seat at this counter.

explanations.answer: So their travels go more smoothly
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the verse isn't about the road. Paul says they put no obstacle in anyone's way, and he says why: “…so that no one can discredit our ministry.” Smooth travel is never mentioned. Save the traffic talk for your commute.

Servants, yes! Verse 4 says, “…as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way…” Paul isn't climbing a ladder here. He's putting on an apron, and I know a thing or two about aprons. Great endurance in troubles, hardships and calamities is how that servant work shows.

I see why that's tempting, baker, since Paul is talking big things about God. But the word in verse 4 is not prophets. He says, “…as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way…” Servants is the title he picks, and he doesn't reach for a fancier one.

Priests sounds official, friend, and I get the pull. But Paul doesn't use that word here. Verse 4 says, “…as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way…” That servant label sits on the whole list that follows.

I can see how it reads that way, baker, because that list is rough. But Paul says the opposite. In verse 3 he wants no one to be able to discredit their ministry, and then he lists beatings, imprisonments and hunger among the ways they commend themselves as servants of God (verses 4-5). So the hard things sit on the commending side of the page. I think this part of the list is heavy, and it's good to slow down for it.

That's the right call, baker. Paul never says these things discredit the ministry. He says, “…as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way…” and the beatings, imprisonments and hunger come inside that list (verses 4-5). It's a heavy stretch of verses. What the text says is that these are part of how they commend themselves.

Purity and kindness, yes. Verse 6 says, “…in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness…” Notice the shift, baker. The list has moved from what comes at them to what shows in how they live. That's a very different kind of list.

Good guess for a list about commending yourself, friend, but fame and influence aren't on it. Verse 6 reads, “…in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness…” Those are about how they live, not how big their name gets. I'll take purity and kindness over a fancy title any day.

Neither of those shows up in verse 6, baker. Paul writes, “…in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness…” Cunning would be a strange fit next to sincere love, which comes right after in verse 6. The right pair is purity and kindness.

explanations.answer: In the right hand and in the left
explanations.explanation: Both hands, baker! Verse 7 says, “with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left…” Nothing is left empty. I've got a mustache for hands, and even I think both is the way to go.

Half right, friend, and half is a lot for one hand. Verse 7 says the weapons of righteousness are carried “…in the right hand and in the left…” Paul doesn't leave the left hand out. Think of someone carrying a laundry basket in each arm.

Interesting pick, baker, but verse 7 doesn't favor one side. It says, “with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left…” Both hands are in the picture. So the left hand isn't carrying this alone.

Praise is it. Verse 8 says, “…through glory and dishonor, slander and praise…” Paul keeps setting opposites side by side, and the pairs keep coming. Slander on one side and praise on the other, and they serve God through both.
Silence is a fair opposite for talk, baker, but it isn't in the verse. Paul writes, “…through glory and dishonor, slander and praise…” Slander pairs with praise. Silence isn't named in this pair.

Threats do sound like they'd travel with slander, friend, but that's not the pair. Verse 8 says, “…through glory and dishonor, slander and praise…” Paul pairs opposites, and the opposite of slander here is praise. Threats aren't named in this verse.

Genuine, baker! Verse 8 says, “viewed as imposters, yet genuine…” People may see them one way, but Paul says what they actually are. I know that feeling. Somebody sees a worn-out stamper and thinks he's done, and they're not looking close.

Rewarded would make a nice ending, friend, but that's not what Paul writes. Verse 8 says, “viewed as imposters, yet genuine…” The pair is imposters against genuine, which is about what they truly are, not a prize they win.

Forgiven is a big, good word, baker, but it isn't the one in this pair. Verse 8 reads, “viewed as imposters, yet genuine…” Imposters is how they're viewed, and genuine is what they are. Forgiven isn't part of this line.

Killed, yes. Verse 9 says, “dying, and yet we live on; punished, yet not killed…” They get punished, but they aren't killed. Paul says it plainly. It's a heavy line, and he states it without dressing it up.

Silenced makes sense in a list like this, baker, but it isn't the word. Verse 9 says, “punished, yet not killed…” Paul doesn't say they were silenced. The pair is about being punished and not being killed.

I get it, baker. Punished and released could go together, but that's not Paul's wording. Verse 9 says, “punished, yet not killed…” Nothing in the line talks about being let go. Killed is the word Paul uses.

That's it, baker! Verse 10 says, “poor, yet making many rich…” They're poor themselves, and still they're making many people rich. That's a puzzle of a pair, and it's one of my favorites. A poor stamper once got called out of a drawer to bake for a feast, so I'm rooting for the poor ones.

Saving up sounds sensible, friend, but that's not what Paul says. Verse 10 reads, “poor, yet making many rich…” The text says nothing about a savings plan. Their story is about the many being made rich.

That would be a natural thing for someone poor to do, baker, but it isn't in the verse. Paul says, “poor, yet making many rich…” He doesn't mention asking anyone for anything. The line is about making many rich.

True, baker! Verse 10 ends with, “having nothing, and yet possessing everything.” Nothing and everything in one breath. That's Paul's whole list landing at once. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer with next to nothing, and I wouldn't trade that line.

Easy to second-guess a line this big, baker. But verse 10 really does say, “having nothing, and yet possessing everything.” Paul isn't dropping the second half. He puts nothing and everything side by side, so True is the answer.

Close, baker, but Paul flips it. Verse 12 says, “It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained.” So the affection being held back is theirs, not his. Paul says his own heart is open wide (verse 11).

That's right, baker. Verse 12 says, “It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained.” Paul says the Corinthians' affection is the restrained one. Right before that, in verse 11, he says, “Our hearts are open wide.”

That's the ask, baker. Verse 13 says, “As a fair exchange—I speak as to my children—open wide your hearts also.” Paul has said his heart is open wide, so he asks theirs to be too. It's a simple request, and a warm one.

A reply would be nice, friend, but the verse doesn't ask for one. Paul says, “As a fair exchange—I speak as to my children—open wide your hearts also.” The ask is about their hearts, not about mail. So no stamp needed.
That's a practical guess, baker, but it's not in verse 13. Paul writes, “…open wide your hearts also.” Travel help isn't mentioned in these verses. The fair exchange he asks for is open hearts.
